Causal learning & simulation across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Abstract thinking (11+ years): Thinking shifts from being tied to physical objects to operating on abstract ideas. Adolescents can reason about concepts that are not directly experienced. A 2026 experiment tests how children generalize patterns (Figure) 67. The authors compare models of pattern generalization (Figure). A cross-cultural study tests induction from action sequences (Figure). The researchers compare features of children’s responses (Figure).

this is effectively where the agent transitions from a system that optimizes known policies within a familiar state space to a system capable of hypothesis testing and zero-shot generalization via structural mapping; there is movement from analyzing things to analyzing the relations between things.

Inductive, deductive, counterfactual, and scientific reasoning; generating and deploying abstract world models

Between 7 and 9, children effectively shift from "piecemeal, premise-by-premise responding" toward "coordinated, model-based inference". They can integrate multiple premises into a coherent whole and have begun to actively search for counterexamples in conditional reasoning tasks. However, these capabilities remain fragile. They are "memory-scaffolded" (mental encoding of relevant states and transitions is unreliable) and heavily reliant on the semantic content of the problem matching the agent’s prior experience. Overall, the 9-year-old is a master of the actual; they reason well about what is, or what is likely to be based on what has been (what has directly presented itself; the concept of "democracy", for instance, tends to escape them). The 12-year-old, conversely, begins their emergence as a master of the possible: the primary computational gain during the 9-12 year window is the decoupling of the internal world model from empirical inputs. This decoupling allows them to perform valid logical operations on hypothetical, indeterminate, and even belief-contradicting premises (including simulating their implications). It is essentially the birth of the "virtual laboratory" within the mind, where variables can be isolated, history can be rewritten (counterfactuals), and future branches can be rigorously stress-tested without the interference of current sensory data or strong semantic priors. As a result, the window between ages 9 and 12 marks a transition from largely instance-bound, association-driven generalization over concrete regularities to increasingly explicit, hypothesis-guided coordination of evidence with abstract causal theories. A 2026 study tests learning and retrieval of related locations (Figure) 66. The study compares memory interference across age groups (Figure).

Inductive reasoning

In terms of inductive reasoning, performance on classic inductive reasoning tasks (often abstract, relational, and IQ-test-like 1, 2) shows steep gains across this period, with the broader developmental curve suggesting that some of the fastest improvements in induction occur from late childhood ( 10-12) into early adolescence ( 12-14), starting in earnest here and accelerating into the 12-14 range 1, 3, 1, 4. These gains are driven in part by better evidence evaluation: children become more sensitive to whether a sample is diverse, representative, and large enough to justify a generalization 5, 6. They also become better at detecting meaningful subcategories within a kind, reflecting advanced conditional modeling ("X is true for this subtype, but not necessarily for all members") 6. A 2025 study examines children’s inductive reasoning (Figure). The study compares reasoning choices across ages (Figure).

These gains are not confined to matrix puzzles and figure analogies; they are increasingly visible in everyday reasoning. Inductive ability in this window is strongly coupled to improvements in fluid intelligence, scientific reasoning, and school achievement in mathematics and science, such that older children’s higher induction scores partly mediate their advantage in STEM learning and complex problem solving 1, 7, 8, 9. In everyday contexts, we can go down the list of behavioral/cognitive advancements that are driven by advanced inductive reasoning. In language, stronger figurative/idiom/proverb understanding reflects causal-pragmatic hypothesis testing about speaker intent and non-literal mappings, and the shift from episodic storytelling to detailed narratives with causal chaining and "global coherence" demonstrates an ability to structure information logically, integrate evidence from real-world episodes, and link events through cause-and-effect frameworks. Reading comprehension also benefits, with 12-year-olds more reliably extracting thematic patterns and inferring character traits from samples across contexts 10. Socially, moral reasoning shifts toward coordinating multiple perspectives (including third-person viewpoints), indicating improved causal attribution across interacting agents and rule-based evaluation of conflicts; the ability to simulate a "neutral observer" view to adjudicate conflicts reflects a detached, quasi-scientific capability to weigh evidence objectively outside of one’s own bias. Self-concept shifts from concrete behaviors to abstract traits/values and children start resolving value conflicts, reflecting principled causal reasoning about motives that generalize across contexts. In the domain of physical objects, the transition to weighting multisensory cues (visual, haptic) based on reliability suggests the brain is adopting a probabilistic, uncertainty-aware approach to inferring latent variables, while strategic switching between thematic and taxonomic classification shows metacognitive control over which inductive scheme fits the causal structure of the task. Spatially, navigation gains (better decisional landmarks, landmark-direction binding, one-trial learning) reflect inductive construction and refinement of causal cognitive maps; the capacity to integrate distinct routes into a survey-like map reflects the logical synthesis of fragmented spatial experiences into a unified global model. Metacognitively, 12-year-olds show a more adult-like ability to evaluate the quality of everyday arguments, for example judging a friend’s decision not to study as a "bad way of thinking" even if it happened to lead to a good grade and explicitly justifying their judgment by appeal to the unreliability of the reasoning process rather than the outcome, reflecting a shift toward process-based, metacognitively monitored induction in everyday scenarios 11, 12. By age 12, then, the typical child’s inductive reasoning has moved from the largely concrete, episodic, and outcome-focused profile of a 9-year-old to a qualitatively more adult-like, explicit, abstract, and process-based system that can monitor sample quality, consider alternative hypotheses, and track causal coherence, even though it still falls short of mature adult induction in reliability, capacity, speed, and domain-generality. The experiment varies the strength of conceptual cues (Figure) 68. The study reports choices with weak cues (Figure).

Deductive reasoning

Deductive reasoning between ages 9 and 12 shifts from a fragile, content-bound competence into the early stages of "true" logical reasoning, where children begin to coordinate multiple premises, detach from immediate belief, and explicitly track logical necessity versus mere plausibility. While younger children rely heavily on heuristic processing, 12-year-olds are much more likely to suppress an immediately compelling but invalid response and instead work through the premises analytically 13, allowing them to construct and test multiple mental models of a problem rather than settling on a single, salient interpretation 14. In conditional reasoning, this shows up as a reduced tendency to "collapse" one-way rules into biconditionals: 12-year-olds are much less likely than 9-year-olds to affirm the consequent (e.g., inferring from "If something is a car, then it has a motor; it has a motor" that it must be a car), with this improvement being particularly noticeable in cases where the antecedent and consequent are strongly associated in semantic memory 15, 16. Across this window, children show a steady increase in their ability to retrieve counterexamples ("things with motors that are not cars") and disabling conditions ("reasons why the usual cause would not produce the effect here") when evaluating "if-then" rules 17, 18. Belief-bias effects are correspondingly weakened: 12-year-olds are more willing to endorse logically valid but factually strange conclusions and to reject believable but invalid ones, indicating that they can let the internal causal/schematic model be constrained by the stipulated premises rather than by their default world knowledge. The same pattern appears in syllogistic reasoning: 12-year-olds are less susceptible to belief bias in classic syllogism tasks, and they are better able to construct and test multiple mental models of the premises ("All A are B; some B are C; what about A and C?"), rather than relying on a single content-driven image 19, 14. On transitive inference and linear-ordering problems with five-term series, performance between 9 and 12 begins to approach ceiling under manageable memory demands: by 12, many children reliably build an ordered internal representation (A>B>C>D>E) and query it flexibly, instead of computing each comparison in isolation, and age differences now look more like differences in strategy and representational load than in basic logical competence 20, 21. A study examines inference while sixth graders read (Figure) 69. The reading study also analyzes sentence-reading time (Figure).

Meta-logically, 12-year-olds display a far more explicit grasp of the various "flavors" of inference, including those based in logical necessity: they differentiate necessary truths (e.g., simple tautologies and arithmetic identities) from empirical regularities and social conventions, judge them as universally and unchangeably true, and increasingly report that they "cannot imagine" a genuine violation, capturing the idea that some conclusions follow in all possible worlds compatible with the premises 22. They are also much better at distinguishing deduction from guessing and from mere perception, at grading the certainty of different knowledge sources, and at explaining in words that "you know that because you figured it out from the rule," not because you saw it; judgments that deduction is more certain than guessing are now backed by explicit reference to inferential structure rather than surface cues 23. Functionally, this makes deduction start to operate as a general-purpose "constraint engine" over internal simulations: given a hypothesis space specified by premises, the 12-year-old can construct and compare alternative possible states of the world, apply abstract if-then rules to those simulated states, and privilege conclusions that are logically necessary within the stipulated model even when they conflict with prior belief or perceptual salience. This competence is, however, still emerging rather than fully mature: belief-bias effects remain robust in many paradigms, especially when propositions are emotionally or socially loaded 24, and 12-year-olds still find it much more demanding to reason with counterfactual causal premises than with familiar factual ones 25. Broadly, conditional reasoning with categorical premises is solid by around 7-8 years, but reliable logical treatment of familiar causal conditionals only becomes typical in the 10-12 range; extending the same level of competence to counterfactual and fully abstract conditionals is more characteristic of mid-adolescence and adulthood 26, 27, 28, 29. In everyday life, the upshot is that a 12-year-old can increasingly treat rules, promises, and causal claims as operators over a space of possibilities, probing "what follows if we all obey this rule?", "what if this assumption is wrong?", or "could both of these stories be true at the same time?", and can call out a peer’s argument as "not making sense" even when the conclusion is attractive, because they are now evaluating the structure of the reasoning rather than just its outcome; a 12-year-old might catch a parent in a contradiction not just by pointing to facts, but by highlighting the flaw in the logic itself ("You said we couldn’t go because of the rain, but now that it’s stopped, you’re changing the rule"), effectively treating the conversation as a system of premises that must remain consistent.

Counterfactual reasoning

Counterfactual reasoning, a form of reasoning in which one contemplates a change to a mental representation and tracks the causal implications of that change 30, is the natural test case for this emerging "virtual laboratory": it is where deductive, causal, and simulational capacities have to be tightly integrated. Structurally, a good counterfactual inference is a constrained deductive inference over an altered world model ("if P had been different, then Q would/would not have occurred"), but computationally it is much harder than the factual cases described above, because the child must maintain at least two models in parallel (the actual and the imagined), decide what to hold fixed, and then propagate the consequences of the stipulated change in a way that respects the underlying causal structure, ultimately allowing the agent to debug past errors and anticipate future regret. Between 7 and 9, children can already answer simple "what if" questions when the story is short, the critical dependency is highlighted, and there is a single, salient causal chain; but they frequently default to basic conditional reasoning (ignoring parts of the actual sequence or overwriting it wholesale) rather than respecting the "nearest-possible-world" constraint, especially when there are multiple potential causes or non-trivial temporal orderings 31. By contrast, during the 9-12 window there is a clear consolidation: counterfactual reasoning starts to look like a general-purpose nearest-world operator rather than a fragile, task-specific strategy; around 12 years, the modal pattern in classic paradigms flips: children now systematically change only those events that are causally downstream of the counterfactual antecedent, keep background conditions fixed, and correctly judge that outcomes with back-up causes would still have occurred if the actual cause were removed, often explicitly justifying their answers with "it would still have happened because …" explanations 32. For comparison, a recent adult experiment isolates hierarchical counterfactual inference (Figure) 71. The study compares computational strategies for the maze (Figure).

Mechanistically, 9- to 12-year-olds become markedly better at keeping the real and imagined worlds apart: whereas many younger children allow counterfactual assumptions to "leak" into their memory for what really happened or confuse actual and imagined details, 11-12-year-olds can track which facts belong to which branch and update only the relevant antecedent in the counterfactual model, a clear sign that the underlying world representation has been decoupled from immediate experience and can be manipulated in a controlled, meta-representational way 33. In everyday life, this manifests as a sophisticated grasp of fault, regret, and relief; a 12-year-old can say "If I had started studying earlier, I would have done better, even if I still passed," or articulate "close calls" ("If I had left one minute later, I would have missed the bus"), utilizing this reasoning to refine future behavior rather than just learning from immediate outcomes. At the same time, important limitations remain. Performance is still highly sensitive to processing load, with long, multiply-caused event chains, deeply counter-to-fact premises, or emotionally charged content leading to systematic errors and outcome-based judgments that resemble those of adults under heavy cognitive load 24, 25. Even by 12, many children focus on a single salient change and neglect less obvious but causally relevant alterations, struggle with nested or iterated counterfactuals ("If she had not believed that…"), and rely heavily on familiar content and story structure. Thus, counterfactual reasoning between 9 and 12 undergoes a qualitative shift from a brittle, context-bound approximation that often collapses back into simple conditional reasoning to an increasingly domain-general, nearest-possible-world operation that can be deployed as a core tool of causal learning and hypothesis testing, but its full flexibility, abstraction, and resistance to belief and emotion-driven distortions continue to develop into mid-adolescence and adulthood.

Scientific reasoning

Scientific reasoning is not a single skill but a coordinated suite of operations over the internal world model: generating hypotheses, designing interventions, representing and aggregating data, evaluating the fit between predictions and outcomes, and regulating all of this with meta-level goals ("what am I trying to find out?") and epistemic norms ("what counts as good evidence?"). Between 9 and 12 these components develop asynchronously and with large individual differences, but the overall profile is clear. Inductive, deductive, and counterfactual reasoning provide the computational "micro-operations" (generalizing from samples; enforcing logical constraints; simulating alternatives); scientific reasoning is the emerging orchestrator that uses those operations intentionally to answer questions about how the world works. This window sees the rapid emergence of the tendency to perform experiments with explicit hypotheses in mind 34, 35, 36, especially in a manner that is cleanly separated from evidence/data (the crucial disentanglement of "theory" and "evidence" 37). On classic paradigms, 9-year-olds may happily manipulate an apparatus and notice regularities, but they typically do so in a way that is driven by curiosity or performance goals without a clearly verbalized "If X, then Y should happen" structure. By 12, a substantial fraction of children will describe their activity in epistemic terms ("I want to see whether this variable matters"), and there is a detectable shift from treating experiments as demonstrations of what one already believes to treating them as tools for inquiry 38. In the words of Deanna Kuhn: "It is the intention to seek knowledge that transforms implicit theory revision into scientific thinking. Theory revision becomes something one does, rather than something that happens to one outside of conscious awareness. To seek knowledge is to acknowledge that one’s existing knowledge is incomplete, possibly incorrect – that there is something new to know." 36

At the level of concrete strategies, the 9-12 window is foremost marked by visible improvements in the control of variables, including in its spontaneous application. Piaget’s classic pendulum problem captures the inflection: while 9- to 10-year-olds typically change string length, bob weight, and release height together and then infer period from the resulting blur of outcomes, around 11-12 years many children begin to systematically vary one factor at a time, holding the others constant, and to reason hypothetico-deductively about which variable the period "must" depend on 39, 40. This control-of-variables strategy is present in rudimentary form much earlier (a 4-year-old can, for example, disambiguate which blocks activate a blicket detector), but the class of systems to which it can be applied expands dramatically: by 12-years-old, children can, say, debug the causal forces in an RC car or a simple aerodynamic system (e.g a kite or a plane) 41, 42 and, overall, 12-year-olds are much better than 9-year-olds at designing controlled, unconfounded experiments, with more demanding assessments often failing to find robust evidence of such competence until around 12 43, 44, 45, 46. Children also become much more sensitive to sample diversity and size; instead of treating "three examples" as intrinsically compelling, they increasingly attend to whether the examples are varied and representative, and they start to articulate why a homogeneous but larger sample may be less informative than a small but diverse one for generalizing to a whole category 5, 6. A longitudinal study tests scientific reasoning in younger children (Figure) 70. The study models the development of scientific reasoning (Figure).

These strategic gains are scaffolded by advances in meta-memory and representational infrastructure. Young children tend to view all strategies in memory tasks as roughly equivalent, and to underestimate both the limits and the malleability of their own cognitive resources. During the first half of this age window ( 9-10), they begin to discriminate between strategies; by age 12, children tend to not only know which strategies (e.g., categorization, rehearsal, external note-taking) are more effective, but also increasingly deploy them spontaneously 47, 48. This period is often described as a qualitative shift in "meta-memory": children come to appreciate that memory is limited and fallible, and that external representational aids (notebooks, tables, diagrams) can and should be used to offload storage and support systematic data recording 49. Concurrent gains appear in their ability to read and construct simple tables and graphs. By 12, most children can interpret basic line graphs and bar charts ("this line goes up, so…") and use them to support inferences, connecting trends or differences in the visualization to underlying causal stories 50, 51. Yet variability and noise remain deeply problematic: children frequently over-interpret single data points, ignore sampling error, and underappreciate the need for repeated trials or larger samples, especially when the data are messy or conflict with their expectations.

Against this backdrop of real progress, the limitations of 9- to 12-year-olds’ scientific reasoning are equally telling. When faced with systems of intermediate or high complexity (multiple variables that combine additively or interactively) most 12-year-olds struggle to generate unconfounded experiments, to disconfirm their own hypotheses, to keep accurate and systematic records, and to integrate results across trials 52, 53, 54, 55. They often test a new idea without checking its compatibility with earlier results 56, or fail to keep records at all, relying instead on noisy impressions of "what seemed to work" 57, 41, 58. Exclusion inferences ("this variable does not have an effect") and judgments of indeterminacy ("this experiment is inconclusive") are especially rare 57, 52. Children in this window, much like adults under strong motivational or cognitive load, tend to treat such outcomes as "failures" rather than as informative constraints on the hypothesis space.

Prior beliefs, goals, and affective stakes continue to exert a strong pull. Although 12-year-olds are markedly better than 9-year-olds at separating theory and evidence as distinct sources of knowledge 59, 49, 60, their experimentation remains highly sensitive to whether they hold strong prior theories and whether the outcomes can be interpreted as positive or negative 60, 61. In many studies, they proceed as though the causal status of a focal variable is already certain and construe the task either as producing the best possible outcome (e.g., building the fastest car) or as accumulating demonstrations that their favored variable "works" across a range of conditions 41, 62, 63, 29, 64. In other words, they readily treat experiments as engineering optimization procedures or as rhetorical tools in service of a prior belief, and only slowly come to view them as impartial tests that could just as well reveal the irrelevance of a cherished factor as its importance. Genuine theory revision (explicitly acknowledging that "what I thought before was wrong" because "the data show something else" and drawing out the downstream implications) remains relatively rare and fragile when it clashes with entrenched prior knowledge 65.

Sophisticated scientific reasoning involves both a toolbox of strategies for hypothesis testing, induction, inference, and evidence evaluation, and a meta-level awareness of when, how, and why to deploy those strategies in the service of knowledge-seeking goals 49. Between 9 and 12, children make major strides across the board: they acquire and refine control-of-variables strategies, become more attuned to diversity, sample size, and subcategories, start to read and construct simple external representations of data, and begin to frame their activity as testing explicit hypotheses rather than merely "trying things out." At the same time, these skills are still highly context-dependent, skewed by prior beliefs and outcome valence, and heavily reliant on scaffolding and relatively simple task structures. By age 12, then, the "virtual laboratory" in the mind has become a partially explicit, self-directed system: children can deliberately set up interventions in their internal and external world models, monitor the resulting data with some appreciation of evidential quality, and use this to revise (or defend) their theories. But the system is still far from adult-like in generality, robustness, or epistemic rigor; what the 9-12 window inaugurates is not mature scientific reasoning, but the onset of formal scientific thought.
